resource-five-minutes-stress.author: Vedanshu
resource-five-minutes-stress.description: Stress has a way of taking over the room.
resource-five-minutes-stress.html:
It can look like racing thoughts, a tight chest, a short temper, or lying awake replaying a conversation from nine hours ago. And when you’re already having a difficult day, most advice about managing stress can feel strangely unrealistic.

  • Take an hour for yourself.
  • Meditate.
  • Go somewhere quiet.
  • Build a routine.

All useful ideas. Not always useful in the moment. Sometimes you have five minutes. That’s enough to start.

What stress is actually doing

Stress isn’t just something you think about. Your body gets involved too.

When something feels threatening or demanding, your body prepares you to respond. Your heart rate can increase, your breathing can become quicker and shallower, and muscles around your shoulders, neck and jaw can tense.

That’s useful when you need to react quickly. It’s less useful when the thing triggering the response is an email, a deadline or a difficult conversation that isn’t going to disappear by running away from it.

If that physical state keeps going for long enough, it can start affecting sleep, concentration, mood and even digestion.

This is one reason “just relax” isn’t particularly helpful advice. You’re asking your mind to calm down while your body is still behaving as though something needs immediate attention.

Sometimes it makes more sense to start with the body.

  • Slow your breathing.
  • Drop your shoulders.
  • Stand up.
  • Walk around for a few minutes.

Give yourself a physical change of state, even if the situation itself hasn’t changed.

Why five minutes can make a difference

You don’t have to solve the thing that’s stressing you before you can feel a little better. The deadline can still be there. The email can still need answering. The conversation can still need having.

The point is to create a little distance between the problem and your immediate physical response to it.

A few slower breaths or a short walk won’t remove the source of stress. They can, however, give you a better place from which to deal with it.

How to make it practical

Don’t try to adopt every technique at once. Pick one.

If you notice your shoulders creeping up towards your ears, take that as a cue to stop for a minute. If your thoughts are running in circles, get up and walk. If everything feels vague and overwhelming, name the actual problem in one sentence.

  • “This email is stressing me out.”
  • “This deadline is making me anxious.”
  • “I haven’t slept properly for three nights.”

One important distinction

A short exercise can help you manage a moment of stress. It isn’t a treatment for ongoing mental health difficulties.

If stress has been sitting with you for weeks, is affecting your sleep or work, or is accompanied by persistent low mood, hopelessness or other symptoms that concern you, it’s worth talking to a doctor or mental health professional. You don’t have to wait until things become unbearable.

The video is a useful place to start. It doesn’t have to be the whole solution.

resource-breathing-five-minutes.author: Vedanshu
resource-breathing-five-minutes.description: Sometimes trying to think your way out of anxiety doesn’t work.
resource-breathing-five-minutes.html:
Your thoughts are already moving too quickly. Trying to reason with every one of them can simply give you more things to think about.

Your breathing is different. It’s automatic, but you can also influence it deliberately. That makes it one of the few parts of your body’s stress response that you can work with directly.

Why focus on breathing?

When you’re anxious, your breathing can become faster or shallower without you really noticing. Paying attention to it gives your mind something concrete to do.

You don’t have to solve anything. You don’t have to work out why you’re anxious. For a few minutes, you just follow the breath.

The recording does the pacing for you, so there’s nothing to memorise and no particular technique you need to get right.

Before you press play

Give yourself five minutes without another task competing for your attention. Sit or lie somewhere comfortable enough that you can let your shoulders relax. Headphones can help, but they’re not necessary. Then press play.

Your mind will wander. That’s normal. The exercise isn’t about keeping your attention perfectly still. When you notice that you’ve wandered, bring it back to the breath. That’s the practice.

What might you notice afterwards?

Don’t look for a dramatic transformation.

  • You might notice that your shoulders feel slightly looser.
  • Your breathing may be slower.
  • Your thoughts might have a little more space between them.
  • You might simply feel a little less wound up than you did five minutes earlier.

That’s enough.

Keep it in perspective

A five-minute breathing exercise isn’t going to resolve ongoing anxiety on its own.

If anxiety is affecting your sleep, work, relationships or everyday activities, or you’re avoiding things you would normally do, it’s worth talking to a doctor or mental health professional. This practice can sit alongside that support. It shouldn’t replace it.

resource-stress-performance.author: Vedanshu
resource-stress-performance.description: A lot of advice about stress falls into one of two categories.
resource-stress-performance.html:
It’s either so general that it’s difficult to do anything with — “take some time for yourself” — or so clinical that you won’t remember it when you’re sitting at your desk with three deadlines and an unanswered message from your manager.

This conversation takes a different route.

Who is Dr. Modupe Akinola?

Dr. Modupe Akinola is a professor at Columbia Business School whose research looks at stress and performance: what happens to people under pressure, how stress affects the way we work and think, and what can change those outcomes.

That makes the conversation particularly relevant to anyone whose stress is closely tied to work. Because workplace stress isn’t an abstract problem.

  • Deadlines.
  • Performance reviews.
  • Difficult colleagues.
  • Unclear expectations.
  • Long hours.
  • The message from your manager that arrives late at night and starts with “quick question.”

Pressure and stress aren’t quite the same thing

Pressure is the situation. The deadline is pressure. The difficult conversation is pressure. The exam is pressure.

Stress is how your mind and body respond to that pressure.

You can’t always remove the pressure. The deadline may be real. The presentation still has to happen. But your response to the situation isn’t necessarily fixed.

That’s where stress research becomes useful. Rather than treating all stress as something that must be eliminated, it asks a more practical question: what happens to us under pressure, and what can actually change that response?

Why this matters at work

Work is one of the places where adults spend a huge amount of time dealing with sustained pressure. And workplace stress can be particularly difficult because avoiding the source isn’t always an option.

You can’t necessarily quit every difficult meeting. You can’t remove every deadline. You can’t control every decision your organisation makes.

Understanding how stress affects attention, judgement and performance can therefore be more useful than being told simply to “avoid stress.”

Give the conversation some time

This isn’t a five-minute exercise. It’s a proper conversation, and it’s better suited to a walk, commute or another stretch of time when you can actually listen. Trying to listen while answering email will probably turn it into background noise.

There is also a reason not to reduce the whole discussion to a handful of motivational takeaways. Stress is complicated. The circumstances that create it are different for different people, and research about groups of people doesn’t automatically tell you what is happening in your own life.

What to take from it

Listen for the distinction between the situation you’re dealing with and your response to it. Notice what happens to your thinking when the pressure increases. And pay attention to which interventions actually seem useful rather than simply sounding useful.

If stress has become your baseline rather than something you move through, that’s worth taking seriously. Particularly if it’s affecting your sleep, mood, relationships or ability to do the things that matter to you.

A podcast can’t assess that for you. A conversation with a doctor or mental health professional can help you work out what to do next.

resource-stress-takes-over.author: Vedanshu
resource-stress-takes-over.description: Stress is part of being human.
resource-stress-takes-over.html:
A difficult deadline, an important decision, uncertainty or a major change can all trigger the body’s stress response. For a while, that’s useful.

Your body becomes more alert. Your heart rate can change. Your breathing can become faster. Your muscles prepare to respond.

The problem isn’t having a stress response. The problem is when it stays switched on long after the immediate situation has passed, or keeps getting triggered over and over.

What happens in the brain?

The amygdala is involved in processing emotional responses to potential threats. Other parts of the brain, including the prefrontal cortex, are involved in things like planning, problem-solving and decision-making.

When you’re under repeated stress, it can become harder to feel calm enough to think clearly.

That doesn’t mean that every stressful day is damaging your brain. It means that prolonged stress can affect how your body and mind feel and function. You might notice it as poor sleep, difficulty concentrating, irritability, physical tension or simply the feeling that you’re never properly switching off.

Why visualisation?

The video introduces guided visualisation as one way of shifting your attention. The idea is straightforward. Picture somewhere that feels calm or safe. It can be somewhere you’ve actually been, or somewhere you create in your imagination.

Then pay attention to the details.

  • What can you see?
  • What can you hear?
  • What does the air feel like?
  • What is beneath your feet?

The point isn’t to pretend that the thing causing your stress has disappeared. It’s simply to give your attention somewhere else to go for a few minutes. Breathing can provide another anchor.

You don’t have to eliminate stress

A completely stress-free life isn’t realistic. The more useful goal is being able to recognise when you’ve been under pressure for too long and knowing how to give yourself some space to recover.

That might be a visualisation like the one in this video. It might be exercise, sleep, time away from work, talking to someone or getting professional support. Different things work for different people.

When it’s time to look beyond self-management

If stress is becoming persistent, increasingly difficult to manage, interfering with sleep or concentration, or making everyday activities harder, don’t assume you simply need to become better at coping.

There may be something worth addressing in the situation itself. And there may be a reason to speak with a qualified professional.

The video is a useful introduction to one technique. It isn’t a treatment or a substitute for professional care.

resource-great-practices.author: Vedanshu
resource-great-practices.description: When stress starts building up, changing your whole lifestyle can feel like one more thing you’re failing to do.
resource-great-practices.html:
It doesn’t have to start that way.

NIMH’s GREAT framework offers five practical places to begin: Gratitude, Relaxation, Exercise, Acknowledge your feelings, Track your thoughts.

You don’t need to do all five.

Gratitude

This isn’t about pretending everything is fine. It’s about noticing something positive or meaningful alongside whatever is difficult.

It could be something small. A person you appreciate. A good conversation. A walk outside. Something you finished. A part of the day that went better than expected.

When stress takes up all your attention, deliberately noticing something else can create a little breathing room.

Relaxation

Your body needs opportunities to come down from a heightened state of alertness. That could mean slow breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery or simply sitting somewhere quiet for a few minutes.

There isn’t one correct way to relax. The useful approach is the one you can actually make part of your life.

Exercise

Movement can help support mental wellbeing. It doesn’t have to mean an intense workout. Walking counts. Stretching counts. Cycling counts. Playing a sport counts. Even finding more opportunities to move during the day can be useful.

Don’t turn exercise into another performance target. Something you can keep doing is generally more useful than something ambitious that lasts a week.

Acknowledge what you’re feeling

Sometimes the first step is simply admitting what’s happening.

  • “I’m worried.”
  • “I’m exhausted.”
  • “I’m angry.”
  • “I’m overwhelmed.”

You don’t have to solve the feeling immediately. Naming it can make it easier to understand what’s behind it and what you might actually need.

Track your thoughts

Stress can produce repetitive thinking. You replay something that happened. You imagine everything that could go wrong. You keep returning to the same problem without getting anywhere.

Writing those thoughts down can make them easier to examine.

  • What am I thinking?
  • What triggered it?
  • Is this something I can influence?
  • Am I treating a possibility as though it’s already a fact?

You don’t have to argue with every thought. Just noticing the pattern can be useful.

Don’t turn this into another checklist

The five ideas are options, not homework. Pick one. Take a walk. Write something down. Spend five minutes breathing. Notice something good. Then see how you feel.

If you’re already overwhelmed, a ten-point self-improvement plan isn’t going to help. Start with one thing.

When you need more than self-management

These are practical ways of managing everyday stress and anxiety. They aren’t a replacement for professional support. If anxiety or stress continues to interfere with your sleep, relationships, work or ability to function, consider talking to a qualified healthcare or mental health professional.

resource-can-we-talk.author: Vedanshu
resource-can-we-talk.description: Sometimes the hardest part of asking for help is starting the conversation.
resource-can-we-talk.html:
You might know that something isn’t right but have no idea how to explain it. You might be worried about being judged. You might think the problem isn’t serious enough. Or you might simply not know what to say.

You don’t need the perfect words.

Start with what you’ve noticed

You can talk about what’s actually been happening without trying to diagnose yourself.

  • “I haven’t been sleeping well.”
  • “I’ve been feeling overwhelmed.”
  • “I don’t feel like myself lately.”
  • “I’m finding it harder to concentrate.”
  • “I’ve been struggling and I don’t really know why.”

That’s enough to start.

If someone comes to you

You don’t need to solve the problem. Listen first. Give them room to explain what they’ve been experiencing.

You can ask:

  • “Do you want to tell me what’s been happening?”
  • “What would be helpful right now?”
  • “Would you like help finding someone to talk to?”

Sometimes that’s more useful than immediately offering advice.

You don’t need certainty before asking for help

A diagnosis isn’t a prerequisite for a conversation. Neither is an assessment result. If something has changed and you’re concerned about it, that’s enough reason to talk to someone.

You can help without taking responsibility for everything

Supporting someone doesn’t mean becoming responsible for fixing their mental health.

  • You can listen.
  • You can help them find information.
  • You can offer practical support.
  • You can encourage them to speak with a professional.

You can also have boundaries around what you can realistically do.

If the first conversation doesn’t go anywhere, that doesn’t mean you have to give up. You can leave the door open. “You don’t have to talk about it now. I’m here if you want to later.” Sometimes that’s enough.

resource-not-always-visible.author: Vedanshu
resource-not-always-visible.description: You can’t always tell how someone is doing by looking at them.
resource-not-always-visible.html:
Someone can be getting through work, meeting friends and answering messages while privately struggling with anxiety, low mood, exhaustion or stress.

Mental health isn’t always visible.

Functioning doesn’t tell you everything

Someone can still go to work while sleeping badly. They can attend a meeting while struggling to concentrate. They can keep up with their responsibilities while feeling completely overwhelmed. They can laugh with friends while having a very different experience once they’re alone.

That doesn’t mean every difficult day is a mental health condition. It means appearances aren’t enough to tell us what someone is experiencing.

Look at the wider pattern

If you’re concerned about yourself or someone else, look beyond whether things appear “fine.”

  • How long has this been going on?
  • Is it getting worse?
  • Is it interfering with everyday life?
  • Has sleep changed?
  • Has the person stopped doing things they normally enjoy?
  • Are relationships being affected?
  • Are they asking for help?

Those questions tell you much more than appearance alone.

If you’re worried about someone

You don’t need to diagnose them. Ask.

  • “How have you actually been doing?”
  • “I’ve noticed you’ve seemed under a lot of pressure lately. Do you want to talk?”
  • “Is there anything I can do?”

Then listen. You don’t have to have the perfect response.

Support can start before certainty

You don’t need to know exactly what’s happening before you take it seriously. If you’re struggling, you can say so. If you’re worried about someone, you can ask.

And if something has been going on for a while or is interfering with everyday life, professional support is worth considering. Mental health doesn’t have to become visible to everyone before it deserves attention.

resource-india-numbers.author: Kartik
resource-india-numbers.description: Most who need care never get it.
resource-india-numbers.html:
On the 29th of May, 2018, The Mental Healthcare Act came into effect. Four years later, to mark Mental Health Day, on 10th October, Tele-MANAS, a national helpline was launched. That has handled over 23.8 lakh calls till now. Today 767 districts are covered under the District Mental Health Programme. All of this indicates some real progress. And yet, this is just scratching the tip of the iceberg. We still have a long way to go. But as the saying goes, well begun is half done.

We have laid the foundation, we are yet to build the structure.

The numbers behind the crisis.

All the data for this piece comes from existing data. We went through the National Mental Health Survey 2015-16 (NIMHANS), the National Crime Records Bureau’s Accidental Deaths and Suicides reports from 2019 to 2023, WHO India, UNICEF, the PIB, and the Economic Survey 2023-24.

The workforce gap is the most damning single figure. The WHO recommends a minimum of 3 psychiatrists per 1,00,000 people. When it comes to clinical therapists, WHO says 1 per 5,000 people. India seriously lags on both accounts with only 0.75 psychiatrists per 1,00,000 and 0.47 psychologists per 5,000 people. To call these deficits would be a massive understatement. These are not mere numbers, for behind these numbers is a very real situation where the only option for someone in crisis is a general physician who may or may not have had any mental health training or worse, no help at all.

The budget tells you where the priority is. On an average, countries spend around 2% of their health budget on mental health. Most public health experts consider this to be quite inadequate. India meanwhile spends just 1%.

Alcohol use disorder affects 4.6% of adults nationally. 86% of those cases go untreated. Among men, the figure is 9.1%. This is not a minor comorbidity; it sits almost entirely outside the formal healthcare system.

The stigma beneath the statistics

Every one of these numbers has a very real human story behind it. Only 10 to 12 percent of people with a mental health condition ever seek any professional help. The remaining never do so. They stay away because seeking help carries social, professional, familial cost. Even when those are not present, many many people cannot afford to pay.

Stigma is not a peripheral problem. It is the reason the treatment gap is 80%. Fix the stigma, and utilisation of whatever services exist climbs. Don’t fix it, and you can build a Tele-MANAS cell in every district and still not reach the people who need it most.

While progress has been made…

The Tele-MANAS helpline with its 53 cells across all the states and union territories is without a doubt a structural achievement. Available in 20 languages it is the first point of contact that didn’t exist a few years ago. The 23.8 lakh calls handled since October 2022 represent 23.8 lakh moments where someone reached out instead of suffering alone.

The Mental Healthcare Act of 2017 reframed mental illness as a rights issue. It mandates insurance coverage, prohibits certain coercive practices, and establishes the right to community-based care. The legal foundation exists even though the implementation is at the moment uneven.

Thankfully all the effort made towards awareness has borne fruit. Roughly 54% of adults now recognise mental illness as a legitimate medical condition, up from around 41%. In a country where the dominant cultural response to psychological distress has historically been to frame it as weakness or family shame, this is not a trivial shift.

…there is still work to be done.

Scale the workforce. The psychiatrist and psychologist deficit cannot be closed quickly, but it can be mitigated by training primary care physicians, ANMs, ASHA workers and volunteers in basic mental health identification and referral. The NMHP’s collaborative care model points in the right direction. It needs resources to match the ambition.

Fund it properly. Mental health spending needs to reach at least 2% of the health budget as an interim target. The Economic Survey has flagged this. It needs to become a budget line, not a recommendation.

Break the stigma systematically. Public communication campaigns, school curricula, and workplace policies all matter. What’s even more effective is visible people speaking openly about their own experiences. I still remember the “2 boond zindagi ke” ads featuring Amitabh Bachchan and Sachin Tendulkar and how successful they were in India’s fight against Polio. Supply-side fixes without demand-side culture change will continue to underperform.

India is not uniquely negligent on mental health. But India’s scale makes the stakes different. Ten percent of 1.4 billion is 140 million people. The numbers are not abstract. They are your colleagues, your relatives, your friends and neighbours. Most of them quietly managing something they feel they cannot name.

The scaffolding is up. It is time to build.

resource-payroll-hidden-cost.author: Kartik
resource-payroll-hidden-cost.description: The most expensive employee problem may be the one that never appears on an invoice.
resource-payroll-hidden-cost.html:
Missed deadlines, resignations, vacant positions, recruitment fees and long periods of sick leave are all visible and generally brought up in budget discussions. Beyond those, however, are signs that are seldom noticed but leave a mark.

An extended leave doesn’t sprout spontaneously. Things begin to go awry well before an employee goes on a mental health break or resigns because of mental health issues. Someone usually checks out well before they even realise it or take steps to rectify it.

The best long-running estimate of what poor mental health costs employers comes from Deloitte, which has repeated the exercise for UK employers since 2017. The 2024 edition puts it at £51 billion a year, down from £55 billion in 2021 but up from £45 billion in 2019. Presenteeism, meaning people at work but not performing at full ability, is the largest part, at roughly £24 billion. A new line in the latest report: working parents’ worries about their children’s mental health cost employers about £8 billion a year in lost productivity, absence and turnover.

Presence is cheaper to miss than absence.

Most managers watch sick days. The research says to watch what happens on days people do come in. Layard’s review finds that between a third and half of all days off work are attributable to mental illness, and in at least 80% of cases it is an underlying condition rather than a bad workplace atmosphere. Presenteeism, studied mostly through self-reported effort, reduces output by at least as much as absenteeism does. Deloitte’s £24 billion for presenteeism supports the same conclusion.

The wider picture is no better. WHO and ILO estimate 12 billion working days a year are lost globally to depression and anxiety, costing nearly US$1 trillion. That is lost output, not employer cost, so it should not be added to Deloitte’s number. Deloitte’s survey also found 63% of respondents with at least one characteristic of burnout, up from 51% in 2021.

Does the investment pay for itself?

The evidence is encouraging, but employers should resist the temptation to promise a guaranteed return.

A 2020 review in The Lancet Psychiatry examined 56 studies of economic evaluations of workplace mental health and substance-use interventions. It found moderate-strength evidence that cognitive behavioural therapy was cost-saving, and in some circumstances cost-effective, for depression.

A separate 2023 systematic review examined 138 workplace prevention interventions across health and safety topics. Of the interventions with reported return-on-investment calculations, 78 had positive results, 12 negative results, 13 neutral results and 35 undetermined results.

That review was not exclusively about mental healthcare. Its findings support the business case for evaluating preventive workplace health programmes, but they should not be presented as proof that 56.5% of mental health programmes generate a positive return.

The distinction matters. Different interventions have different costs, different outcomes and different levels of supporting evidence. A programme that improves health may still be worthwhile even if its direct financial savings do not exceed its cost.

Some examples of what prevention looks like.

resource-country-development.author: Kartik
resource-country-development.description: A country’s mental health is an economic asset. We should start treating it like one.
resource-country-development.html:
Words like GDP growth, industrial output, exports, employment and infrastructure are everyday words. You’ll see them in the news and on social media every day. Oftentimes, these come up in our mealtime conversations. Mental health, on the other hand, barely features in the same conversations, unless a crisis makes it impossible to ignore.

This at times proves to be a pretty costly omission.

If a struggling person can’t access appropriate support, the consequences can be far-reaching. They do not end with their symptoms. These have the ability to affect a great deal of other things, like whether that person completes their education, enters the workforce, keeps a job, earns a stable income or supports their family. Across a population, this individual health problem becomes a development challenge.

The economic case for mental healthcare is not that every person must be productive to deserve support. It is that avoidable suffering also creates avoidable barriers to participation, opportunity and economic security.

The price of leaving mental health underfunded.

The McKinsey Health Institute’s 2025 analysis, developed with the Clinton Health Access Initiative, estimates that mental health conditions account for approximately 290 million disability-adjusted life years* (DALYs) globally. Despite this staggering amount, mental health receives only about 2% of domestic government healthcare spending worldwide. This figure, according to most estimates, is highly inadequate. The report estimates an annual global mental health investment gap of US$200 billion to US$350 billion, depending on the scale of intervention coverage pursued.

What about India, one may ask? India spends just about half of the global average. A mere 1%. We have had a few successful interventions like Tele-MANAS, a mental health helpline which has handled around 3 million calls, and even there the budget has been cut while demand is growing.

These gaps indicate a mismatch between the scale of the problem and the resources directed towards tackling it. What must be kept in mind is that not all countries have the same funding gap. In addition to this, what also needs to be noted is that spending alone does not guarantee better outcomes.

Along with the funding itself, we also need to evaluate whether the funding is reaching the right places and measures. Measures such as prevention, early intervention, treatment and recovery support.

The economic consequences are far-reaching and wide.

According to the WHO, mental health costs a country an average of 4% of its GDP. Mental health affects an economy in more than one way, often through multiple connected channels.

The return on investment is worth taking seriously.

According to the McKinsey Health Institute, cost-effective mental health interventions could generate up to US$4.4 trillion in additional global economic value by 2050. They also estimate that each US$1 invested in scaling these interventions could produce US$5–US$6 in economic returns, measured through GDP growth. The World Health Organization reached similar conclusions. Its 2016 global investment case for scaling up treatment for depression and anxiety estimated a US$147 billion investment requirement over 2016–2030. The study projected US$399 billion in productivity gains from treating depression and anxiety, alongside substantial health benefits.

While they estimate different returns, both highlight the importance of providing effective care. They emphasise the need to change how governments across the world see mental healthcare. Instead of treating it like a recurring cost which needs to be absorbed, it needs to be treated as an investment in the country’s growth.

Prevention flips the economics.

McKinsey’s model finds that scaling proven interventions to 90% coverage could avert 150 million DALYs in 2050, add 1.1 years of healthy life per person and return $5 to $6 of GDP per dollar invested. Its authors note that treatment dominates their result (over 82% of the impact) mainly because treatment has more published trials.

The prevention evidence that does exist is mostly from the UK. A Department of Health and LSE review found that each £1 spent on parenting programmes to prevent conduct disorder saves about £8 over the child’s lifetime. It also found that each £1 spent on early intervention for first-episode psychosis saves about £18. A later Public Health England tool estimated £1.58 returned per £1 on a whole-school anti-bullying programme over four years. Those are modelled returns, not guarantees, and they vary a lot by programme. Even so, none of them is a loss.

Measure what improves, not just what gets spent.

Mental health budgets should be assessed against outcomes that matter. Shorter delays before treatment, fewer avoidable interruptions to education and work, better recovery, reduced financial hardship and more equitable access to care.

The strongest economic argument for mental healthcare is not that a person becomes more valuable when they return to work. It is that preventable illness should not deprive people of the opportunity to learn, earn, participate and live well.

A country cannot develop to its full potential while leaving a substantial part of its population without the support needed to participate in society. Mental health deserves a place in development policy not as an afterthought to economic growth, but as one of the conditions that makes lasting growth possible.

The policy choice is not between economic development and mental healthcare. It is whether development plans account for the health of the people expected to sustain them.

*Disability-adjusted life year (DALY). A disability-adjusted life year is a measure of overall disease burden, representing a year lost due to ill-health, disability, or early death.

resource-india-open-data.html:
This article presents an overview of mental health in India based on publicly available data from national surveys, government budgets, and crime records. It examines prevalence, access to care, demographic disparities, and the economic burden of mental illness.

The scale of the challenge

  • The National Mental Health Survey (NMHS 2015–16), conducted by NIMHANS, remains India’s only nationally representative mental health survey. It found 10.6% of adults had a diagnosable mental disorder at the time of the survey, and 13.7% had experienced one in their lifetime.
  • The same survey estimated that nearly 150 million Indians require active mental health care, while fewer than 30 million were receiving it. A treatment gap exceeding 80%, rising to over 90% for some disorders.
  • The rural–urban divide is quite stark, with prevalence being roughly twice as high in urban areas (13.5%) as in rural areas (6.9%).
  • No updated nationally representative survey has been published since 2015–16. More recent figures rely on programme data (Tele-MANAS), NCRB suicide statistics, and smaller regional studies. A staggering data gap in itself.

There are mental health disparities among demographic cohorts. By gender, women report depression and anxiety symptoms at 2–3x the male rate, while men carry far higher rates of substance use disorders. By age, adolescent prevalence (7.3% in 2015–16) is rising faster than any other cohort, and suicide is now the leading cause of death for Indians aged 18–30. By geography, the four states of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu account for over a third of all student suicides.

Access is the binding constraint.

We are training fewer psychiatrists and psychologists than we need. We have ~9,000 practising psychiatrists for a population of 1.4 billion people. We need around 36,000 to hit WHO’s minimum benchmark of 3 per 1,00,000 (the global average is 4.7). This is only compounded by India’s inadequate funding of mental healthcare.

Spending has held at roughly 1% of the total health budget for three straight years, with over 90% concentrated in two centrally funded institutes. The global average for spending on mental healthcare is 2% of the total health budget. Most experts agree 2% is an extremely low amount.

Psychiatrists aren’t the only shortage.

India’s talk-therapy workforce, i.e. psychologists and counsellors, is proportionally even thinner.

According to the RCI (Rehabilitation Council of India), India has 4,309 registered clinical psychologists for all of India, plus 801 rehabilitation social workers. Most talk therapy is provided by clinical psychologists and general counsellors. Since there is no single mandatory licensing body for general counsellors, quality and availability vary widely by region.

Recently two new rules have been passed which will test this gap. In 2026 CBSE amended its affiliation bye-laws making it mandatory for every school to have a Counselling & Wellness Teacher, at a ratio of one per 500 students in classes 9–12. Prior to 2026, only schools with more than 300 students had to follow this rule.

Taking note of the campus suicides, the Supreme Court has made the UGC mandate one trained counsellor per 100 students in universities and colleges.

Both these guidelines highlight and acknowledge that India does not currently have enough trained counsellors to fill these mandated roles, particularly outside large cities.

Youth mental health is worsening fastest.

Student suicides have climbed for three straight years, reaching a decade high in 2024.

1 in 7 adolescents in India aged 10–19 faces a mental health condition. Most of them either get inadequate care or rarely get any care at all. This is an entire generation of young adults who will grow up with untreated mental health issues.

All of this comes at an extremely steep cost.

Poor mental health is expensive for everyone.

The costs aren’t limited to productivity and employers alone; even individuals have to bear a steep price because of inadequate care. Unchecked mental health issues can lead to chronic physical health issues like heart disease, which require lifelong care and expenses. For those who already have an existing physical health condition, untreated mental health issues make things exponentially worse. According to a study, people with mental health comorbidities consume 60% more resources and have a 50% higher mortality rate.

Sources

Primary data sources

  • NIMHANS Bengaluru (2015–16). National Mental Health Survey of India (opens in a new tab), commissioned by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare.
  • National Crime Records Bureau (2021–2024). Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India (ADSI) (opens in a new tab). Ministry of Home Affairs.
  • Ministry of Health & Family Welfare / PIB (2022–2025). Tele-MANAS programme data and press releases (opens in a new tab).
  • Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (FY2022–23 to FY2025–26). Union Budget documents (opens in a new tab).
  • Rehabilitation Council of India. Central Rehabilitation Register (opens in a new tab), clinical psychologist and social worker counts.
  • CBSE, UGC and the Supreme Court (2026). CBSE affiliation bye-law circulars (Jan 2026) and UGC/Supreme Court mental-health staffing guidelines.

Supporting sources

  • WHO. Mental Health Atlas.
  • Indian Journal of Psychiatry. ‘Women and Mental Health in India’ and workforce studies.
  • Deloitte India (2022). ‘Mental Health and Well-being in the Workplace’ survey.
  • Ministry of Finance (2025). Economic Survey of India 2024–25.
  • UNICEF (2021). Adolescent mental health survey data, State of the World’s Children.
  • Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health & Family Welfare (2023). Report.
  • Indian Psychiatric Society (2024). Adolescent stress and anxiety study.
  • DataM Intelligence (2026). India Mental Health Market report.
  • Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research (LISER). The economics of mental health (opens in a new tab).

A note on the data. India has no annual, standardised mental-health data. Figures here are drawn from the most recent official release for each indicator and therefore span different reference years (NMHS: 2015–16; NCRB and Tele-MANAS: 2021–2025; budgets: FY2022–26; school/campus mandates: 2026). The 2022 student-suicide figure is derived proportionally from a published percentage share. This is an independent synthesis of public data and does not represent the official position of any institution named above.

98d536d4-938b-4fbf-bc2c-f37e6d0b9409.html:
Don't want to read all that, don't worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The BAT-23 is a 23-question screening tool that measures burnout across four core symptoms which are, exhaustion, mental distance, cognitive impairment, and emotional impairment on a 5-point frequency scale. It screens for burnout but does not diagnose it. Physical and cognitive symptoms can overlap with medical conditions. Also, written by humans.

What is the BAT-23?

Burnout has traditionally been measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), a 22-item tool built in 1981 around workplace cynicism. In 2019, researchers Wilmar Schaufeli, Hans De Witte, and Steffie Desart at KU Leuven in Belgium set out to build something broader and freely available. They reviewed more than 300 items across dozens of existing burnout questionnaires and interviewed working professionals to figure out what burnout actually feels like day to day. The result was the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT-23) which treats cognitive problems (trouble focusing, forgetfulness) and emotional problems (irritability, losing emotional control) as core symptoms of burnout in their own right, not just side effects.

Things to know about the BAT-23.

  • Number of questions: 23
  • Duration: About 5 minutes
  • Timeframe: General/recent experience
  • Scale: 1 to 5 per item
  • Dimensions: 4 core symptom clusters

What does the BAT-23 actually measure?

The BAT-23 groups its 23 items into four core symptoms of burnout:

  • Exhaustion: feeling physically and mentally drained, struggling to recover
  • Mental distance; cynicism, detachment, or aversion toward your work
  • Cognitive impairment: trouble concentrating, remembering things, or thinking clearly
  • Emotional impairment: feeling unable to control emotional reactions, irritability, tearfulness

How is the BAT-23 scored?

Each item is rated on how often it applies to you:

  • Never: 1 point
  • Rarely: 2 points
  • Sometimes: 3 points
  • Often: 4 points
  • Always: 5 points

Item scores are averaged within each of the four dimensions, and the four dimension scores are then combined into an overall burnout score.

What does my BAT-23 score really mean?

The researchers behind the BAT-23 deliberately built it to support clinical cutoffs, something older burnout scales were criticized for lacking. Using data from thousands of employees across multiple European countries, they came up with three bands.

  • Low: no significant signs of burnout
  • Moderate: at risk of burnout, worth paying attention to
  • Red: scores consistent with severe burnout, professional support recommended

Some things to keep in mind about the BAT-23.

The BAT-23 is a screening tool, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE.

Burnout is not currently classified as a standalone medical diagnosis, though the WHO recognizes it as an occupational phenomenon.

Some symptoms of burnout overlap with other issues, so please speak to a doctor in case the symptoms persist or are unmanageable. Symptoms like persistent exhaustion, trouble concentrating, irritability, and emotional flooding could also be caused by issues such as:

  • Depression or an anxiety disorder
  • Thyroid disorders like hypothyroidism
  • Sleep disorders like sleep apnea or insomnia
  • Iron-deficiency anemia
  • ADHD (for concentration and memory symptoms specifically)

Just so you know.

1b783468-f860-433b-8009-7e7943321ac1.description: Stress of the job can take a heavy toll, this questionnaire helps you understand how.
1b783468-f860-433b-8009-7e7943321ac1.html:
For the times you just want a TL;DR version for you: The Workplace Stress Scale is a quick, 8-question self-assessment tool (scored 8–40) created by The Marlin Company and the American Institute of Stress. It measures how much stress you experience on the job and your risk of work-related burnout. Scores of 21 or higher suggest moderate to severe workplace stress that may require lifestyle changes or workplace adjustments. It measures job strain, not a clinical psychiatric condition. Also, written by humans.

What is The Workplace Stress Scale?

Workplace stress is one of the leading contributors to employee burnout, lower productivity, and reduced physical health. To help individuals and organizations spot stress early, The Marlin Company collaborated with The American Institute of Stress (AIS) to develop The Workplace Stress Scale.

Unlike clinical anxiety or depression tools, this questionnaire focuses specifically on environmental and organizational factors such as workload, control, job security, and workplace support and gives a quick snapshot of how your job is impacting your overall well-being.

Things to Know About The Workplace Stress Scale

  • Number of questions: 8
  • Duration: 1–2 minutes
  • Timeframe: General (how you typically feel about your current job)
  • Maximum Score: 40
  • Minimum Score: 8
  • Scale: 1 to 5 (Likert Scale)

What Does The Workplace Stress Scale Actually Measure?

The scale's questions assess key dimensions of work life, including:

  • Workload & Demands: Feeling overwhelmed by tasks, deadlines, or unrealistic expectations.
  • Control & Autonomy: Having little say over how you perform your work or manage your time.
  • Job Security & Stability: Worrying about layoffs, restructuring, or future employment.
  • Workplace Relationships: Feeling unsupported by management or experiencing friction with colleagues.
  • Work-Life Balance: Difficulty disconnecting from work during personal time.

How is The Workplace Stress Scale Scored?

For each of the 8 statements, you rate how frequently you feel a certain way on a 5-point scale:

  • 1 Point: Never
  • 2 Points: Rarely
  • 3 Points: Sometimes
  • 4 Points: Often
  • 5 Points: Very Often

Your total score is calculated by adding up all 8 item scores, resulting in a final score between 8 and 40.

What Does My Score Really Mean?

Since workplace stress is an occupational hazard rather than a medical illness, your score helps categorize your current stress risk level:

Score

Stress Level

What It Means & Suggested Next Steps

8–15

Low / Relatively Calm

You experience low workplace stress. Your job environment is likely manageable, and your coping strategies are working well.

16–20

Fairly Low

You encounter occasional work stressors, but they are generally under control. Practice routine self-care to maintain balance.

21–25

Moderate

Work stress is starting to accumulate. You may feel frequent fatigue or frustration. Next steps: Re-evaluate your boundaries, delegate tasks where possible, and build recovery time into your week.

26–30

Severe

You are experiencing high workplace stress and are at a significant risk for burnout. Next steps: Speak with your manager, HR, or a career mentor to address workload concerns, or seek guidance from a professional.

31–40

Potentially Dangerous

Extremely high workplace stress. This level of strain often bleeds into physical health and personal life. Immediate intervention is recommended. Consider taking time off, consulting a healthcare provider, or seeking professional support.

Some Things to Keep in Mind About The Workplace Stress Scale

  • It is an occupational assessment; IT DOES NOT DIAGNOSE MENTAL HEALTH DISORDERS.
  • High work stress can contribute to anxiety or depression, but the scale itself simply measures job strain.
  • Workplace stress manifests physically. Chronic job stress often triggers physical symptoms like tension headaches, gastrointestinal trouble, elevated blood pressure, fatigue, or insomnia.
  • Stress is a two-way street. While individual coping strategies (mindfulness, exercise, time management) help, structural issues like poor management, understaffing, or toxic culture require workplace-level solutions.
  • Physical health conditions can lower your stress tolerance. Underlying issues like thyroid imbalances, vitamin deficiencies, or chronic pain can make standard workloads feel significantly more overwhelming.

Just So You Know

Mental health landscape continues to evolve, one approach is gaining traction for its ability to drive better patient outcomes: measurement-based care (MBC). In this blog post, we'll delve into the world of MBC, exploring its definition, benefits, and real-world applications in mental health.

What is Measurement-Based Care?

Measurement-based care is an approach to healthcare that leverages data and measurement tools to inform treatment decisions. In the context of mental health, MBC involves using standardized assessments and outcome measures to track patient progress, identify areas of improvement, and adjust treatment plans accordingly.

The Benefits of Measurement-Based Care in Mental Health

So, why is MBC such a game-changer for mental health? Here are just a few benefits:
  1. Improved patient outcomes: By using data to inform treatment decisions, clinicians can tailor their approach to each patient's unique needs, leading to better outcomes.
  2. Enhanced patient engagement: MBC empowers patients to take a more active role in their care, fostering a sense of ownership and motivation.
  3. Increased efficiency: By streamlining the assessment process, clinicians can reduce administrative burdens and focus on what matters most: providing high-quality care.

How Measurement-Based Care Works

So, how does MBC work in practice? Here's a step-by-step overview:

  1. Initial assessment: Patients complete a standardized assessment, which provides a baseline measurement of their symptoms and functioning.
  2. Ongoing measurement: Patients complete regular assessments, which track their progress and identify areas of improvement.
  3. Data analysis: Clinicians review the data, using it to inform treatment decisions and adjust the care plan as needed.
  4. Treatment adjustment: Based on the data, clinicians make adjustments to the treatment plan, ensuring that patients receive the most effective care possible.

Real-World Applications of Measurement-Based Care

MBC is already being used in a variety of mental health settings, from private practices to hospitals and clinics. Here are just a few examples:

  1. Depression treatment: MBC can help clinicians identify the most effective treatment approach for patients with depression, reducing symptoms and improving quality of life.
  2. Anxiety disorders: By tracking patient progress and adjusting treatment plans accordingly, MBC can help clinicians provide more effective care for patients with anxiety disorders.
  3. Substance abuse treatment: MBC can help clinicians identify the most effective treatment approach for patients with substance use disorders, reducing relapse rates and improving long-term outcomes.

Measurement-based care is revolutionizing the mental health landscape, providing clinicians with the data-driven insights they need to deliver more effective care. By embracing MBC, clinicians can improve patient outcomes, enhance patient engagement, and increase efficiency. As the mental health community continues to evolve, one thing is clear: measurement-based care is here to stay.

Don’t want to read all that, don’t worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The GAD-7 is a quick, 7-question screening tool (scored 0–21) used to measure anxiety severity based on symptoms over the past two weeks. Scores of 10 or higher suggest significant anxiety that warrants professional evaluation. It screens for symptoms but does not diagnose. Physical anxiety symptoms can overlap with medical conditions. Also, written by humans.

What is GAD-7?

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is one of the most common mental disorders with up to 20% of adults being affected by it each year. In 2006 researchers Robert L. Spitzer, Janet B.W. Williams, Kurt Kroenke, and Bernd Löwe created GAD-7 which today is widely used by psychiatrists and therapists to figure out the severity and probable causes of anxiety and also to track how the treatment is progressing.

Things to know about GAD-7.

  • Number of questions: 7
  • Duration: 1-2 minutes
  • Timeframe: 2 weeks
  • Maximum Score: 21
  • Scale: 0 to 3

What does GAD-7 actually measure?

GAD 7’s questions are designed to look at these factors like:

· Worry

· Being on edge

· Physical restlessness

· Sense of dread like something is about to go wrong

· Short fuse

· Inability to unwind

· Real world impact of anxiety

How is GAD-7 scored?

Depending on what you respond to each question, the responses are marked on a scale of 0-3. The maximum score for GAD 7 is 21.

The possible responses are as such:

· Not at all: 0 points

· Several Days: 1 point

· More than half the days: 2 points

· Nearly every day: 3 points

GAD 7 is finally scored by adding up all the points, going up to 21.

What does my GAD-7 score really mean?

There is no official score which means you have GAD, but clinicians generally set the benchmark at 10. In case you score 10 or above, it would mean you need to speak to an expert and explore further evaluation.

Depending on the score, your anxiety could fall in one of these bands:

Score

Severity

Next Steps

0-4

Minimal

Normal anxiety, no clinical intervention required.

5-7

Mild

Slightly elevated anxiety, nothing to worry about. Practice wellness and self-monitor. Retake GAD-7 in 2 weeks.

8-9

Moderate

Noticeable worry, Practice wellness and self-monitor. Retake GAD-7 in 2 weeks.

10-14

Moderately Severe

Significant anxiety, further evaluation by an expert required.

15-21

Severe

Extremely high, active treatment needed.

Some things to keep in mind about GAD-7.

The GAD-7 is a screening tool, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE.

Some symptoms of GAD overlap with other issues, please speak to a doctor in case the symptoms persist or are unmanageable.

Symptoms like chronic exhaustion, persistent muscle stiffness, twitching or trembling, shortness of breath, palpitations, lightheadedness and nausea could be because of issues such as:

· Thyroid disorders like hypothyroidism

· Fibromyalgia

· Heart issues like cardiac arrhythmias

· Lung issues like asthma, COPD

· Gastrointestinal issues like IBS, peptic ulcers

Just so you know.

11457137-5bba-4f45-9d0d-51d7e2a4c9c6.description: Why do we monitor our bodies but ignore our minds? Explore the ROI of "Digital Zen" and how to start measuring your mental health for a high-vibe life.
11457137-5bba-4f45-9d0d-51d7e2a4c9c6.html:
For the past few years I have been getting regular health check ups. Someone with diabetes will check their sugar frequently, watch their weight and take steps in case the parametres don’t look good. People struggling with blood pressure will monitor it. When it comes to our physical health, we're accustomed to regular check-ups, screenings, and tests to monitor our well-being. We vital signs to catch any potential issues before they become major problems.

What about our mental health? Why don't we prioritize measuring and monitoring our mental well-being with the same rigor as our physical health?

The Logic of Enlightenment: Why We Measure

Quantifying the mind isn't about labels; it’s about light. Bringing data into the conversation is the ultimate tool for a balanced life. Here’s why we do it:

  1. The Early Warning System: Just like a weather report helps you prepare for a storm, monitoring your mental vitals lets you spot the clouds before they break. By identifying shifts early, we can pivot with precision, staying ahead of the curve and keeping our inner peace intact.
  2. A Blueprint for Your Unique Self: There is no "one size fits all" in Zen. By measuring our mental landscape, we create a custom roadmap tailored to our specific needs. This data-backed approach ensures that every step we take is the most effective one for our personal journey.
  3. Normalizing the Invisible: When we treat the mind with the same analytical respect we give the body, the shadows of stigma start to fade. Measuring mental health sends a clear, powerful signal: your internal world isn't a secret to be kept—it’s a vital part of your health to be mastered.

The Dividends of Digital Zen

Measuring the mind isn't just about data—it’s about the "ROI" of inner peace. Here is how the math adds up to a better life:

  1. Precision Well-being: Just as a heart rate monitor guides an athlete, regular mental metrics lead to better outcomes. When we track the "vitals" of our mood, symptoms lose their mystery and the quality of our daily life climbs.
  2. Empowered Ownership: Data turns you from a passenger into the pilot. When you can actually see your mental patterns, you’re more likely to take the wheel, stay engaged, and make lifestyle shifts that actually stick.
  3. A Smoother Path to Care: Measurement cuts through the "noise." By turning subjective feelings into clear insights, we streamline the journey to wellness, removing the guesswork and letting everyone focus on what matters: high-impact healing.
  4. The Ultimate Wealth—Wellness: The math of mindfulness is undeniable. According to the WHO, every $1 invested in mental health yields a $4 return in health and productivity. By catching "glitches" early through data, we bypass the high cost of burnout and trade it for a sustainable, high-vibe life.

Mapping Your Inner Miles: How to Begin

Ready to upgrade your internal dashboard? Integrating mental vitals into your routine is simpler than you think. Here is how to start the "data-informed" journey:

  1. The Gold Standard Tools: Just as we use a scale or a blood pressure cuff, we can use verified "Internal Thermometers" like the PHQ-9 or GAD-7. These aren't just tests; they are standardized snapshots that turn complex feelings into actionable insights.
  2. The Digital Zen Toolbox: Leverage the power of the tech in your pocket. From mood-tracking apps to biofeedback platforms, digital tools allow you to log your "state of mind" in real-time, creating a high-definition map of your well-being that you can share with your care team.
  3. The Ritual of the Check-In: Data is most powerful when it’s consistent. By scheduling regular "System Reviews" with a professional, you ensure your roadmap is always up to date. These check-ins allow you to tweak your settings and adjust your path before you ever wander off track.

Measuring mental health is essential for maintaining good mental well-being, identifying early warning signs of mental health conditions, and developing personalized treatment plans. By prioritizing mental health measurements, we can reduce stigma, improve patient outcomes, and enhance the overall quality of care.

Let's treat mental health with the same importance as physical health. It's time to make mental health measurements a priority.

4a4ac2b7-17be-4e9e-9d8e-7d244af5aa73.author: Kartik
4a4ac2b7-17be-4e9e-9d8e-7d244af5aa73.description: Stop waiting for a crisis to prioritize your mind. Learn how routine mental health check-ups help you manage stress, build resilience, and show up as your best self.
4a4ac2b7-17be-4e9e-9d8e-7d244af5aa73.html:
Mental health is just as essential as physical health, yet many of us neglect to prioritize it. Routine mental health check-ups are crucial for maintaining good mental wellness, preventing mental health issues, and promoting overall well-being. In this post, we'll explore the importance of routine mental health check-ups and why they should be a non-negotiable part of our self-care routine.

Why Checking In With Your Mental Health Is the Ultimate Flex

Think of routine mental health check-ups as the "preventative maintenance" for your life, rather than just a crisis response. By catching the small stuff before it spirals into a chronic condition, you’re essentially fortifying your future self. These check-ins do more than just flag potential issues; they serve as a dedicated space to sharpen your self-awareness and build a toolkit of strategies that keep you resilient. Beyond the personal benefits, prioritizing these check-ins helps strip away the outdated stigma that mental health is something to hide, making it as normal as going to the dentist or the gym. Because your mind and body are on the same team, keeping your head in a good space directly fuels your physical energy, ensuring you're showing up as the best version of yourself in every room you walk into.

Benefits for Specific Groups.

  1. Young Adults: Routine mental health check-ups can help young adults navigate the challenges of transitioning to independence, managing academic pressures, and developing healthy relationships.
  2. Working Professionals: Regular check-ups can provide working professionals with strategies for managing work-related stress, improving work-life balance, and maintaining productivity.
  3. Parents and Caregivers: Mental health check-ups can offer parents and caregivers guidance on managing the emotional demands of caregiving, prioritizing self-care, and maintaining their own mental wellness.

Making Your Mind a Priority: A Guide to Consistent Care

The first step to prioritizing your mental health is treating it with the same logistical respect you give your physical body. Start by finding a professional you actually click with—someone whose style aligns with your personality—and then lock in those sessions as non-negotiable appointments on your calendar. It’s not just about showing up, though; the real progress happens when you’re willing to be open and honest about what’s actually going on under the hood. When you pair these professional check-ins with daily self-care habits like getting outside, moving your body, or practicing mindfulness, you create a sustainable ecosystem for your brain to thrive in.

Investing in these routine check-ups is a proactive move that pays dividends across your entire life. By catching small stressors before they escalate, you’re not just preventing burnout; you’re actively sharpening your self-awareness and boosting your physical energy. This consistency helps normalize the conversation around mental health, proving that seeking support is a sign of strength rather than a last resort. Ultimately, treating your mental well-being as a high priority ensures that you stay resilient, self-aware, and ready to handle whatever life throws your way, leading to a much healthier and more balanced version of yourself.

a9697070-1dff-4bcc-a67d-2fbb26cc6e25.description: Unlock the benefits of the PHQ-9 for healthcare, the workplace, and personal growth. Reduce absenteeism, improve productivity, and streamline mental health care.
a9697070-1dff-4bcc-a67d-2fbb26cc6e25.html:
TL;DR because we get it, sometimes we also just want to take a glance and get the gist of something: The PHQ-9 is a 9-question screening tool (scored 0–27) used to measure depression severity based on symptoms over the past two weeks. Scores of 10 or higher suggest significant depression that warrants professional evaluation. It screens for symptoms but does not diagnose. Physical depression symptoms can overlap with medical conditions. By the way this is written by humans.

What is PHQ-9?

Major depressive disorder is a common mental health condition affecting millions of adults worldwide each year. In 1999, researchers Kurt Kroenke, Robert L. Spitzer, and Janet B.W. Williams developed the PHQ-9 (as part of the broader Patient Health Questionnaire) to assist clinicians in rapidly assessing the presence and severity of depressive symptoms and tracking treatment progress over time.

Things to know about PHQ-9.

  • Number of questions: 9
  • Duration: 1-3 minutes
  • Timeframe: Past 2 weeks
  • Maximum Score: 27
  • Scale: 0 to 3

What does PHQ-9 actually measure?

PHQ-9’s questions align with the diagnostic criteria for major depression and look at factors like:

  • Little interest or pleasure in doing things
  • Feeling down, depressed, or hopeless
  • Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much
  • Feeling tired or having little energy
  • Poor appetite or overeating
  • Feeling bad about yourself or that you are a failure
  • Trouble concentrating on things
  • Moving or speaking slowly, or being unusually fidgety/restless
  • Thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself

How is PHQ-9 scored?

Depending on your response to each question, the items are marked on a scale of 0–3:

  • Not at all: 0 points
  • Several days: 1 point
  • More than half the days: 2 points
  • Nearly every day: 3 points

Once the responses have been recorded, all points are added up to get a score which ranges from 0 to 27.

What does my PHQ-9 score really mean?

There is no official score which diagnoses one with depression, however a score of 10 or above is generally accepted by practitioners to recommend further evaluation.

  • The PHQ-9 is a screening tool—it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE.

  • Symptoms of depression frequently overlap with physical medical conditions. Persistent physical complaints should be evaluated by a physician.

Physical symptoms such as chronic fatigue, changes in sleep or weight, brain fog, and psychomotor changes can stem from underlying medical issues like:

  • Thyroid dysfunction like hypothyroidism
  • Vitamin deficiencies of Vitamin D, and B12

c775a1e1-a938-4aac-8519-e5ad9f8dda1f.description: Take control of your rest! Discover the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI), a simple assessment to help you understand your sleep patterns and unlock better quality sleep.
c775a1e1-a938-4aac-8519-e5ad9f8dda1f.html:
Don’t want to read all that, don’t worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The SCI is an 8-item screening tool (scored 0–32) designed to evaluate insomnia severity and sleep quality based on DSM-5 criteria over the past month. Lower scores indicate worse sleep, with a score of 16 or below suggesting potential clinically significant insomnia. It screens for symptoms but does not diagnose. Physical sleep issues can overlap with underlying medical or psychiatric conditions. As it is with all our blogs, this too is written by humans.

What is the SCI?

Insomnia and poor sleep quality affect a huge portion of the adult population, impacting overall health, focus, and mood. Developed in 2014 by researchers Colin A. Espie and colleagues, the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI) was created as a reliable, standard screening instrument based directly on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) criteria for insomnia disorder. Today, it is widely used by researchers, doctors, and clinicians to screen for insomnia, measure sleep impairment, and track treatment progress over time.

Things to know about the SCI.

  • Number of questions: 8
  • Duration: 2–3 minutes
  • Timeframe: Past 1 month
  • Maximum Score: 32
  • Scale: 0 to 4 per item

What does the SCI actually measure?

The SCI's questions are designed to look at these factors like:

  • Nighttime symptoms (time taken to fall asleep, nighttime awakenings)
  • Overall sleep satisfaction and quality
  • Daytime functioning and energy levels
  • Impact of sleep issues on mood, focus, or productivity
  • Duration of sleep problems (how many months it has been an issue)
  • Number of nights per week sleep is affected

How is the SCI scored?

Depending on what you respond to each question, the responses are marked on a 0–4 scale (with specific descriptions tailored to each question). The maximum total score for the SCI is 32.

Unlike many mental health tools where a higher score means higher severity, the SCI is scored such that lower numbers indicate poorer sleep quality and higher risk for insomnia.

What does my SCI score really mean?

Clinicians generally set the cutoff benchmark at 16 or lower to flag potential insomnia. If you score 16 or below, it suggests that your sleep troubles are likely impacting your daily life and warrant further evaluation by a specialist.

Depending on the score, your sleep condition could fall into one of these bands:

Score

Severity

Next Steps

0–16

Probable Insomnia / Severe Impairment

Significant sleep difficulties; further evaluation by a sleep specialist or doctor is recommended.

17–24

Moderate Sleep Disturbance

Noticeable sleep disruption or daytime impact; focus on sleep hygiene and monitor over the next few weeks.

25–32

Minimal / Good Sleep

Normal sleep patterns with no significant clinical impairment required.

Some things to keep in mind about the SCI.

The SCI is a screening tool; it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE.

Poor sleep can be caused or compounded by other medical or psychiatric conditions. Please speak to a doctor if sleep problems persist.

Symptoms like chronic daytime exhaustion, loud snoring, gasping for air at night, restless legs, or severe night sweats could be because of issues such as:

  • Sleep disorders like Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) or Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS)
  • Thyroid dysfunction (e.g., hyperthyroidism)
  • Chronic pain conditions
  • Circadian rhythm disorders or shift work disorder
  • Mood disorders such as depression or generalized anxiety

Just so you know.

de31d473-fda7-47e4-82d6-a549b02eec44.description: Master your stress with the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS). Learn how this 10-item assessment improves self-awareness, boosts productivity, and enhances well-being.
de31d473-fda7-47e4-82d6-a549b02eec44.html:
Like us in case you too would like a TL;DR version, we've got your back: The PSS-10 is a quick, 10-question tool (scored 0–40) that measures how unpredictable, uncontrollable, and overloaded you've felt your life to be over the past month. Widely circulated bands describe 0–13 as low, 14–26 as moderate, and 27–40 as high stress. It screens for perceived stress but does not diagnose anything. Physical stress symptoms can overlap with medical conditions. BTW, all of the information here is written by a human.

What is the PSS-10?

In 1983, psychologist Sheldon Cohen, along with Tom Kamarck and Robin Mermelstein, published the Perceived Stress Scale to measure how stressful a person's life felt to them. The PSS is designed around the belief that two people can perceive the exact same circumstances entirely differently. It's since become one of the most widely used psychological instruments for measuring stress, in both research and clinical settings.

Things to know about the PSS-10.

  • Number of questions: 10
  • Duration: 2–5 minutes
  • Timeframe: 1 month
  • Maximum Score: 40 Scale: 0 to 4

What does the PSS-10 actually measure?

The PSS-10's questions are designed to look at how you've felt over the past month, including:

  • Feeling upset by something unexpected
  • Feeling unable to control important things in your life
  • Feeling nervous or "stressed"
  • Feeling confident about handling personal problems
  • Feeling things are going your way
  • Feeling on top of things
  • Being able to control irritations
  • Feeling on top of things vs. feeling things are piling up

How is the PSS-10 scored?

Each item is rated on how often it applied to you over the past month:

  • Never: 0 points
  • Almost Never: 1 point
  • Sometimes: 2 points
  • Fairly Often: 3 points
  • Very Often: 4 points

Questions 4, 5, 7 and 8 are scored in reverse. For these questions the range is 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0. All scores are added up and with the maximum possible score being 40.

What does my PSS-10 score really mean?

As with most scales there's no official clinical cutoff. A set of bands has become widely circulated online and in some clinical materials, even though they aren't formally endorsed by the scale's developer:

Low: Score below 13

Moderate: Between 14 and 26

High: Anything above 40

Some things to keep in mind about the PSS-10.

The PSS-10 is a screening tool, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE.

Perceived stress is shaped by whatever's happening in your life at the moment. What that means is your score today is significant till the next 4-6 weeks, post which conditions might have changed.

Some symptoms linked to chronic stress overlap with other issues, so please speak to a doctor in case the symptoms persist or are unmanageable. Symptoms like persistent fatigue, sleep disruption, muscle tension, headaches, and stomach upset could also be caused by issues such as:

  • Thyroid disorders like hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism
  • An anxiety disorder or depression
  • Chronic pain conditions like fibromyalgia
  • Gastrointestinal issues like IBS
  • Sleep disorders like insomnia or sleep apnea

Just so you know.

resource-who-5.author: Kartik
resource-who-5.description: The WHO-5 is a 5-question well-being check scored 0-100. It measures how you have actually felt over the past two weeks, not what is wrong with you.
resource-who-5.html:
Don't want to read all that? Don't worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The WHO-5 is a quick, 5-question self-assessment tool scored from 0 to 100. It measures positive mental well-being and general quality of life over the past two weeks. While lower scores (below 50) indicate reduced well-being and may suggest the need to check for burnout or depression, it is a wellness screener, not a standalone diagnostic test. Also, written by humans.

What is the WHO-5?

First introduced in 1998 by the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Europe, the WHO-5 Well-Being Index is one of the most widely used global measures of subjective mental health.

Unlike many clinical questionnaires that focus on symptoms of mental illness, fear, or distress, the WHO-5 focuses entirely on positive mental well-being, looking at your energy, relaxation, mood, and interest in daily life. It is frequently used in corporate wellness programs, coaching, routine healthcare checkups, and personal wellness tracking.

Things to know about the WHO-5.

  • Number of questions: 5
  • Duration: 1 minute
  • Timeframe: Past 2 weeks
  • Maximum Score: 100 (percentage score)
  • Minimum Score: 0
  • Scale: 0 to 5 per question

What does the WHO-5 actually measure?

The WHO-5's questions focus on five core pillars of positive mental state experienced over the past two weeks:

  • Positive Mood: feeling cheerful and in good spirits.
  • Calmness: feeling calm, relaxed, and unbothered.
  • Vitality and Energy: feeling active and vigorous.
  • Restful Sleep: waking up feeling fresh and rested.
  • Life Engagement: feeling that daily life is filled with things that interest you.

How is the WHO-5 scored?

For each of the 5 statements, you choose how often you felt that way over the past two weeks:

  • All of the time: 5 points
  • Most of the time: 4 points
  • More than half of the time: 3 points
  • Less than half of the time: 2 points
  • Some of the time: 1 point
  • At no time: 0 points

Calculating your final score: add up your responses to get a raw score between 0 and 25, then multiply the raw score by 4 to convert it to a standard percentage score between 0 and 100. For example, a raw score of 15 x 4 = 60%.

What does my WHO-5 score really mean?

Higher scores mean higher subjective well-being. While there is no official "pass/fail", healthcare professionals and researchers generally categorise the scores as follows:

Score

Well-Being Level

What it means and next steps

72-100%

High Well-Being

You are experiencing strong positive energy, vitality, and life engagement. Keep up your current routines.

52-68%

Moderate Well-Being

Reasonable well-being, though there may be room to improve sleep, stress management, or daily balance.

28-48%

Low Well-Being

Significantly reduced emotional energy. Consider practicing self-care, reducing stress, or taking a secondary screener (like the PHQ-9).

0-24%

Very Low Well-Being

Extremely depleted well-being. It is recommended to speak with a healthcare provider or professional for an evaluation.

Some things to keep in mind about the WHO-5.

  • The WHO-5 is a well-being screener, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE MENTAL DISORDERS. A low score indicates low mood or energy, not an automatic clinical diagnosis.
  • It focuses on health, not just illness. By measuring positive states rather than negative symptoms, it helps spot early signs of emotional burnout before severe problems develop.
  • Low well-being can stem from physical factors. Physical fatigue, nutrient deficiencies, thyroid issues, poor sleep hygiene, or viral recovery can drop your score drastically without a psychological root cause.
  • It is great for tracking progress. Taking the WHO-5 every 2 to 4 weeks allows you to monitor how lifestyle changes, therapy, or work adjustments impact your overall quality of life over time.

Just so you know.

resource-ngse.author: Kartik
resource-ngse.description: The NGSE is an 8-question scale that measures how much you believe you can handle what you set out to do. It is a mindset measure, not a clinical test.
resource-ngse.html:
Don't want to read all that? Don't worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The New General Self-Efficacy (NGSE) scale is a quick, 8-question self-assessment tool (scored 8-40) designed to measure your belief in your ability to achieve goals and overcome challenges. Scores of 32 or higher indicate high general self-efficacy. It measures personal confidence and mindset, not a psychological disorder or medical condition. Also, written by humans.

What is the NGSE?

Self-efficacy refers to your confidence in your ability to perform tasks, solve problems, and handle life's obstacles. In 2001, researchers Gilad Chen, Stanley Gully, and Dov Eden created the New General Self-Efficacy (NGSE) Scale to improve upon earlier self-efficacy questionnaires. Unlike domain-specific tools (which focus only on work, sports, or academics), the NGSE measures your overall baseline belief in yourself across a wide variety of everyday situations.

It is widely used in personal development, executive coaching, workplace training, and research to help individuals understand their self-belief profile and build resilience.

Things to know about the NGSE.

  • Number of questions: 8
  • Duration: 1 to 2 minutes
  • Timeframe: General (how you feel about your capabilities overall)
  • Maximum Score: 40
  • Minimum Score: 8
  • Scale: 1 to 5 (Likert scale)

What does the NGSE actually measure?

The NGSE's questions are designed to look at factors such as:

  • Goal Attainment: confidence in achieving goals you set for yourself.
  • Problem-Solving and Adaptability: belief in your ability to overcome unexpected obstacles.
  • Task Mastery: confidence that you can perform tough tasks effectively.
  • Resilience and Recovery: the capacity to bounce back after facing difficulties or setbacks.
  • General Confidence: an overall sense of capability across diverse areas of life.

How is the NGSE scored?

For each of the 8 statements, you rate how much you agree or disagree on a 5-point scale:

  • Strongly Disagree: 1 point
  • Disagree: 2 points
  • Neither Agree nor Disagree: 3 points
  • Agree: 4 points
  • Strongly Agree: 5 points

The final NGSE score is calculated by adding up the points from all 8 questions, giving you a total score between 8 and 40.

What does my NGSE score really mean?

Since the NGSE is a self-assessment tool, not a clinical diagnostic test, there is no rigid "pass/fail" or diagnostic threshold. However, your score helps indicate where your current level of self-efficacy falls.

Some things to keep in mind about the NGSE.

  • The NGSE is a self-reflection tool, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE ANY MENTAL HEALTH CONDITION. Low general self-efficacy is a mindset trait, not a clinical illness.
  • Self-efficacy is dynamic, not fixed. Your score can change over time depending on life circumstances, stress levels, recent accomplishments, or personal growth work.
  • Self-efficacy is different from self-esteem. Self-esteem is about how much you value yourself; self-efficacy is about how much you believe in your ability to execute tasks.
  • If low self-confidence is accompanied by persistent feelings of hopelessness, burnout, or severe anxiety, it may be beneficial to speak with a mental health professional or career coach for personalised support.

Just so you know.
