resource-brs.author: Kartik
resource-brs.description: The BRS is a 6-question scale that measures one thing only: how quickly you bounce back after stress. It is scored as an average, not a total.
resource-brs.html:
Don't want to read all that, don't worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The BRS is a quick, 6-question self-assessment that measures how well you bounce back from stress and hardship, scored on a 1-5 average. Scores below 3 suggest lower resilience, 3 to 4.3 is typical, and above 4.3 is considered high resilience. It screens for a general tendency, not a fixed trait, and it does not diagnose anything. Also, written by humans.

What is the BRS?

Most resilience scales at the time were built to measure resilience indirectly, by looking at things like social support, optimism, or personal resources that are thought to help someone cope. In 2008, researchers Bruce W. Smith, Jeanne Dalen, Kathryn Wiggins, Erin Tooley, Paulette Christopher, and Jennifer Bernard set out to measure something more specific: how quickly and completely someone actually recovers from stress. Their tool, the Brief Resilience Scale, has since become one of the most widely used short resilience measures in both research and everyday self-assessment, precisely because it's fast and gets straight at the "bounce back" idea people usually mean when they talk about resilience.

Things to know about the BRS.

  • Number of questions: 6
  • Duration: 1 to 2 minutes
  • Timeframe: General, not tied to a specific period
  • Scale: 1 to 5
  • Score type: Average (not a sum)

What does the BRS actually measure?

The BRS's six statements are designed to look at:

  • How quickly you bounce back after hard times
  • How much difficulty you have getting through stressful events
  • How long it takes you to recover from a stressful event
  • How hard it is to "snap back" when something bad happens
  • How smoothly you get through difficult times
  • How long it takes you to get over setbacks

Three of the six items are worded positively (like bouncing back quickly) and three are worded negatively (like having a hard time getting through stress), which helps balance out response bias.

How is the BRS scored?

Each statement is rated on how much you agree with it:

  • Strongly Disagree: 1 point
  • Disagree: 2 points
  • Neutral: 3 points
  • Agree: 4 points
  • Strongly Agree: 5 points

The three negatively worded items are reverse-scored before totaling. Unlike scales that add everything up into one big number, the BRS is scored as an average: add up all six item scores and divide by 6. That gives you a final score somewhere between 1 and 5.

What does my BRS score really mean?

The BRS doesn't have a diagnostic cutoff, but the scale's creators and later research commonly use these bands to interpret the average score:

Score

Resilience Level

Next Steps

1.00-2.99

Low resilience

May be worth building coping skills, support, or stress-management habits.

3.00-4.30

Normal resilience

Typical range for most adults, nothing to be concerned about.

4.31-5.00

High resilience

Strong tendency to bounce back from stress and hardship.

Some things to keep in mind about the BRS.

The BRS is a self-report screening tool, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE anything, and it isn't meant to measure your worth or resolve as a person. It measures your general tendency to recover from stress, not the specific tools or resources you have to do so (things like social support or coping strategies aren't captured here). A low score doesn't mean something is wrong with you; it can reflect anything from a genuinely rough stretch of life to simply not having had much practice bouncing back yet.

If low resilience is showing up alongside ongoing low mood, hopelessness, or exhaustion that doesn't let up, it's worth talking to a doctor or therapist, since those patterns can overlap with issues such as:

  • Depression or an anxiety disorder
  • Burnout
  • Chronic stress or an ongoing crisis
  • Sleep deprivation, which affects coping capacity broadly

Just so you know.

resource-gad-2.author: Kartik
resource-gad-2.description: The GAD-2 is the first two questions of the GAD-7, used as a 30-second check. A score of 3 or more is a signal to look closer, nothing more.
resource-gad-2.html:
Don't want to read all that, don't worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The GAD-2 is an ultra-quick, 2-question screening tool (scored 0-6) derived from the first two items of the GAD-7. It measures core anxiety symptoms over the past two weeks. A score of 3 or higher indicates a positive screen, suggesting that a fuller evaluation (like completing the full GAD-7 or speaking to a doctor) is warranted. It screens for symptoms but does not diagnose. Also, written by humans.

What is the GAD-2?

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) affects millions of adults worldwide. In 2007, researchers Kurt Kroenke, Robert L. Spitzer, Janet B.W. Williams, and colleagues developed the GAD-2 as an ultra-brief first-step screening tool. Because full assessments can take time, doctors and clinics often use the GAD-2 as a rapid pulse-check during routine visits to catch potential anxiety early.

Things to know about the GAD-2.

  • Number of questions: 2
  • Duration: Under 1 minute
  • Timeframe: Past 2 weeks
  • Maximum Score: 6
  • Scale: 0 to 3

What does the GAD-2 actually measure?

The GAD-2 isolates the two core psychological symptoms of generalized anxiety:

  • Nervousness: feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge.
  • Uncontrollable Worry: not being able to stop or control worrying.

How is the GAD-2 scored?

Depending on how often you were bothered by each symptom over the last 2 weeks, responses are scored from 0 to 3:

  • Not at all: 0 points
  • Several days: 1 point
  • More than half the days: 2 points
  • Nearly every day: 3 points

Adding the points for both questions gives a final score between 0 and 6.

What does my GAD-2 score really mean?

Unlike the GAD-7, which breaks anxiety into multiple severity bands (mild, moderate, severe), the GAD-2 functions as a go / no-go flag. Its purpose is simply to decide whether further evaluation is needed.

Score

Result

Next Steps

0-2

Below Threshold

Anxiety symptoms are minimal or below the typical screening cutoff. No clinical evaluation usually required unless you feel distressed.

3-6

Positive Screen

Indicates significant core anxiety symptoms. The recommended next step is to take the full GAD-7 or discuss your results with a healthcare professional.

Some things to keep in mind about the GAD-2.

  • The GAD-2 is an initial screening tool, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE. A score of 3 or more means "look closer", not "you have an anxiety disorder".
  • It misses physical symptoms and specific phobias. Because the GAD-2 focuses heavily on worry and generally feeling on edge, it can miss panic attacks, PTSD, or purely physical manifestations of anxiety (racing heart, trembling, nausea).
  • Physical symptoms overlap with medical conditions. Physical anxiety symptoms like palpitations, shortness of breath, or fatigue can stem from medical issues such as thyroid conditions, asthma, or cardiac arrhythmias.
  • If you're struggling, trust yourself regardless of the score. Even if you score below a 3, reach out to a professional if anxiety is interfering with your work, sleep, or personal life.

Just so you know.

resource-phq-2.author: Kartik
resource-phq-2.description: The PHQ-2 asks two questions about mood and interest. It is a triage step, not a diagnosis, and a positive screen points you to the full PHQ-9.
resource-phq-2.html:
Don't want to read all that, don't worry, we got a TL;DR version for you: The PHQ-2 is an ultra-quick, 2-question screening tool (scored 0-6) derived from the full PHQ-9. It measures core depressive symptoms over the past two weeks. A score of 3 or higher indicates a positive screen, suggesting that a fuller evaluation (like completing the full PHQ-9 or speaking to a medical professional) is needed. It screens for symptoms but does not diagnose. Physical conditions can also cause similar symptoms. Also, written by humans.

What is the PHQ-2?

Depression is one of the most common medical conditions worldwide, yet it often goes unnoticed during standard doctor visits. In 2003, researchers Kurt Kroenke, Robert L. Spitzer, and Janet B.W. Williams developed the PHQ-2 as a rapid first-step screening tool.

By using just two targeted questions, doctors, clinics, and health systems can rapidly evaluate patients during routine checkups to determine if a deeper conversation about mood is necessary.

Things to know about the PHQ-2.

  • Number of questions: 2
  • Duration: Under 1 minute
  • Timeframe: Past 2 weeks
  • Maximum Score: 6
  • Scale: 0 to 3

What does the PHQ-2 actually measure?

The PHQ-2 isolates the two core diagnostic symptoms of major depression:

  • Anhedonia: having little interest or pleasure in doing things you usually enjoy.
  • Depressed Mood: feeling down, depressed, or hopeless.

How is the PHQ-2 scored?

Depending on how often you were bothered by either problem over the last 2 weeks, responses are scored from 0 to 3:

  • Not at all: 0 points
  • Several days: 1 point
  • More than half the days: 2 points
  • Nearly every day: 3 points

Adding the points from both questions gives a final score between 0 and 6.

What does my PHQ-2 score really mean?

Like the GAD-2, the PHQ-2 functions primarily as an initial triage tool rather than a full severity scale. Its main goal is to identify who needs follow-up screening.

Score

Result

Next Steps

0-2

Negative Screen

Low risk of major depression. No immediate clinical intervention required unless you feel distressed.

3-6

Positive Screen

Significant core depressive symptoms present. The recommended next step is to take the full PHQ-9 or consult a healthcare professional.

Some things to keep in mind about the PHQ-2.

  • The PHQ-2 is a screening tool, it DOES NOT DIAGNOSE. A score of 3 or higher indicates a need for further evaluation, not an automatic diagnosis of clinical depression.
  • It focuses only on the core symptoms. It leaves out secondary symptoms of depression like sleep disturbances, appetite changes, fatigue, or low self-worth (which are covered in the 9-item PHQ-9).

Depressive symptoms can also overlap with physical health conditions. Chronic exhaustion, low motivation, and low mood can be caused or aggravated by underlying medical issues like:

  • Hypothyroidism or endocrine imbalances
  • Vitamin deficiencies (such as Vitamin D or B12)
  • Anemia
  • Chronic fatigue syndrome or neurological conditions

Always seek help if you are struggling. Regardless of your score, if you are experiencing persistent low mood or thoughts of self-harm, reach out to a trusted doctor or mental health professional immediately.
